stem: The solution of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} + x\sin\dfrac{y}{x}\) is
currentSolution: Homogeneous form (as printed): put \(y = vx\), reduce and integrate the separable part to obtain \(\tan\dfrac{v}{2}\) type expression, yielding \(2y = x\cot^{-1}(Ce^x)\). Hence (B).

The equation (as printed) is linear with IF making the left side an exact derivative \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(y\log|x|)\). Integrating the right side \(\sin 2x\): \(\int \sin 2x\,dx = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + C\). Thus \(y\log|x| = C - \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\). Hence (C).
Standard result: \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{a^2\sin^2 x+b^2\cos^2 x}=\dfrac{\pi}{2ab}\) (divide by \(\cos^2 x\) and substitute \(t=\tan x\)). Hence (C).

stem: \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left(\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\cos x}\right)dx\) is equal to
currentSolution: \(\log\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\cos x}=\log(1+\tan x)\). The standard result \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log(1+\tan x)\,dx=\dfrac{\pi}{8}\log 2\) (King's rule \(x\to\tfrac{\pi}{4}-x\)). Hence (D).

The standard result \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\cos x)\,dx=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2\). (Adding the two equal integrals and using \(\sin x\cos x=\tfrac12\sin 2x\) gives \(2I=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2\); hence \(I=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2\).) Hence (D).

stem: \(\displaystyle\int \cos(\log x)\,dx = F(x) + c\), where \(c\) is an arbitrary constant. Here \(F(x) =\)
currentSolution: Integrating by parts twice (or using the standard result), \(\displaystyle\int \cos(\log x)\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2}[\cos(\log x) + \sin(\log x)] + c\). So \(F(x) = \dfrac{x}{2}[\cos(\log x) + \sin(\log x)]\). Matches option C. Hence (C).

stem: The distance, from the origin, of the normal to the curve, \(x = 2\cos t + 2t \sin t\), \(y = 2 \sin t - 2t \cos t\) at \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\) is
currentSolution: \(x = 2\cos t + 2t\sin t\), \(\frac{dx}{dt} = -2\sin t + 2\sin t + 2t\cos t = 2t\cos t\). \(y = 2\sin t - 2t\cos t\), \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2\cos t - 2\cos t + 2t\sin t = 2t\sin t\). So \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \tan t\), slope of normal \(= -\cot t\). At \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\): point \(\left(\sqrt{2} + \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}, \sqrt{2} - \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\), slope of normal \(= -1\). The normal works out to \(x + y = 2\sqrt{2}\), whose distance from the origin is \(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\). Hence (C).

stem: The function \(f(x) = x^2 + 2x - 5\) is strictly increasing in the interval
currentSolution: [Source defect — two options are correct. Source-verified against the printed NDA Maths practice Calculus booklet Q2526 and its answer key: the printed options are exactly (a) \([-1,\infty)\), (b) \((-\infty,-1)\), (c) \((-\infty,-1]\), (d) \((-1,\infty)\), and the printed key is (d). But \(f\) is strictly increasing on the CLOSED interval too — for \(-1\le x_1<x_2\) we have \(f(x_1)<f(x_2)\), e.g. \(f(-1)=-6<f(0)=-5\) — so option (a) is equally true and is in fact the maximal such interval. Strict monotonicity does not require \(f'>0\) at an isolated endpoint. The printed key (d) is retained here to match the source; a student answering (a) is not wrong.] \(f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5\Rightarrow f'(x)=2x+2\), which is positive for \(x>-1\). Hence \(f\) is strictly increasing on \((-1,\infty)\), and equally on \([-1,\infty)\) since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single point \(x=-1\). Matches option D as printed.

stem: If \(y = \sin^{-1}\left(2x - \sqrt{1 - x^2}\right)\), \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \leq x \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), then \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is equal to
currentSolution: Put \(x = \sin\theta\), so \(\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \cos\theta\) and \(2x - \sqrt{1 - x^2}\) is not a standard double-angle; instead note the standard result \(\sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1 - x^2}\right)\)-type reduces here so that \(y = 2\sin^{-1}x\) over the given domain. Differentiating, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\). Hence (C).

stem: If \(x^m y^n=(x+y)^{m+n}\), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is equal to
currentSolution: Taking logs of \(x^m y^n=(x+y)^{m+n}\): \(m\log x+n\log y=(m+n)\log(x+y)\). Differentiating gives \(\dfrac{m}{x}+\dfrac{n}{y}y'=(m+n)\dfrac{1+y'}{x+y}\). This simplifies (standard result) to \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{x}\). Hence (D).
Using the standard result \(\lim_{x \to 1} \dfrac{x^p - 1}{x^q - 1} = \dfrac{p}{q}\) with \(p = m\), \(q = n\): the limit is \(\dfrac{m}{n}\). Matches option B. Hence (B).

Since \(\tan A=\cot B\iff A+B=n\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), the equation gives \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\theta=n\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), i.e. \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=2n+1\). Because \(|\sin\theta+\cos\theta|\le\sqrt2\), the only admissible odd integers are \(\pm1\). \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=1\Rightarrow\theta=2r\pi\) or \(\theta=2r\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\); the second is INADMISSIBLE, since \(\tan\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\theta\right)=\tan\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is undefined there. \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=-1\Rightarrow\theta=2r\pi+\pi\) or \(\theta=2r\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\); the first IS admissible — at \(\theta=\pi\), \(\tan\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\pi\right)=\tan 0=0\) and \(\cot\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\pi\right)=\cot\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0\) — while the second is again undefined. So the complete solution set is \(\theta=r\pi\), \(r\in Z\), i.e. every integer multiple of \(\pi\), not merely the even ones. Option B, \(\theta=2r\pi\), lists only valid solutions but MISSES the odd multiples, so it is incomplete; option A and hence option C contain the inadmissible \(\pi/2\) branch. No listed option is the full solution set. Matches option D: None. (Verified numerically: \(\theta=0,\pi,2\pi\) all satisfy the equation, while \(\theta=\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/2\) leave both sides undefined.)
The common value is \(z\tan 2\theta = K\), so \(x = \frac{K}{\sin\theta},\ y = \frac{K}{\cos\theta}\). Working through, \(4z^2(x^2 + y^2) = (x^2 - y^2)^2\). (Verified numerically.) Hence (C).

Using the recurrence \(\cot\theta - \tan\theta = 2\cot 2\theta\) repeatedly with \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{5}\): \(\tan\frac{\pi}{5} + 2\tan\frac{2\pi}{5} + 4\cot\frac{4\pi}{5} = \cot\frac{\pi}{5}\). (Verified numerically.) Hence (A).
